chapter_summary:
Lighting is arguably the most crucial element in making your scenes look believable and visually appealing. It defines mood, highlights important details, and reveals the form and texture of your models. In Houdini, just like in the real world, light sources emit photons that interact with your materials, and a renderer calculates how these interactions produce the final image. Understanding the different types of lights and how to control their properties is fundamental to achieving professional-looking renders. Houdini provides several essential light types, each suited for different purposes.

The most common light types you'll encounter are:
*   **Point Light:** Emits light uniformly in all directions from a single point, similar to a bare light bulb. It's excellent for general illumination, small sources, or simulating omnidirectional light.
*   **Spot Light:** Emits light in a cone shape, allowing you to direct light to specific areas, much like a flashlight or stage light. It has parameters for cone angle and penumbra angle (feathering at the edge).
*   **Area Light:** Emits light from a defined surface (e.g., a rectangle, disc, or sphere). Area lights produce softer, more realistic shadows than point or spot lights because the light source has a physical size. They are commonly used to simulate windows, softboxes, or large diffuse light sources.
*   **Environment Light:** This is a powerhouse for realistic, image-based lighting. Instead of a single point or area, an `Environment Light` uses a **High Dynamic Range Image (HDRI)** wrapped around your scene to provide complex, real-world lighting and reflections. HDRIs capture the full range of light intensities from a real location, allowing for incredibly accurate global illumination and reflections. They are often the first light you'll add to a scene to establish a realistic base lighting environment.

To add lights, you'll typically do so in the `obj` context. Select `Lights and Cameras` from the top menu, or press `Tab` in the network editor and type `light`. Once a light is created, its parameters panel offers extensive controls. Key parameters include `Color` (the hue of the emitted light), `Intensity` (the brightness, often measured in lumens or candelas for physical accuracy), and `Exposure` (an f-stop-like control for overall brightness). For physically accurate lighting, you'll want to pay attention to `Decay`. Real-world light intensity diminishes with distance. Most lights in Houdini default to `Quadratic Decay`, meaning light intensity falls off with the square of the distance, which is physically correct. Disabling decay or setting it to `None` will result in unrealistic, infinitely bright light.

When working with an `Environment Light`, the most important parameter is the `Map` or `Environment Map` where you load your HDRI file. You can find many free HDRIs online (e.g., Poly Haven, HDRI Haven). Once loaded, the HDRI will illuminate your scene and provide realistic reflections on metallic or glossy surfaces. You can rotate the `Environment Light` to change the direction of the dominant light source, and adjust its `Intensity` or `Exposure` to control the overall brightness. For game development, HDRIs are often baked into light probes or irradiance volumes within the game engine, but in Houdini, they provide an excellent way to preview and render assets under realistic conditions.

A common challenge in complex scenes is controlling which lights affect which objects. This is where **light linking** comes in. By default, all lights affect all objects. However, you might want a specific light to only illuminate a character, or exclude a background object from a certain fill light. In Houdini, you can access light linking through the `Light Linker` panel (Windows > Light Linker). Here, you can create relationships between lights and objects, specifying which lights are included or excluded for a given object. This gives you granular control over your lighting setup, allowing for artistic direction and optimization. For example, you could have a strong key light for your main character, but exclude it from the background to avoid overexposure, and then use a separate, softer fill light for the background. This selective illumination is crucial for achieving polished renders and optimizing render times by avoiding unnecessary light calculations. Always remember to consider the purpose of each light in your scene – is it a key light, fill light, rim light, or bounce light? Each plays a role in defining the overall look.

screens.title: Lighting Fundamentals in Houdini
screens.subtitle: How light types, HDRIs, and light linking shape believable renders

narration.text: In this lesson we'll build a mental model of lighting in Houdini and why it is the most powerful tool for shaping mood and realism. We'll look at the core light types you will use every day — point, spot, area, and environment — and learn how their physical properties like decay, exposure and size change shadows and reflections. You will also see how an HDRI environment light adds realistic global illumination and how light linking gives you precise control when a scene has many elements. For example, a single HDRI can add coherent long-range reflections and soft ambient fill while a nearby area light sculpts a soft key that reveals form. Knowing which light to use and which parameters to adjust saves render time and prevents a flat, overexposed image. As we proceed, think about the role each light plays: key light defines form, fill light softens shadows, rim light separates subjects, and environment light provides context. By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up a three-point lighting rig augmented by an HDRI and selectively link lights to objects for artistic control. Keep in mind a common misconception: bigger intensity isn't always better — size, decay and exposure interact and must be balanced for believable results. Ready to explore the practical steps and examples?

keyIdea.title: Why lighting matters
keyIdea.text: Lighting defines form, mood, and realism. Use the right light type and parameters to reveal materials and control reflections without overexposing the scene.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use while lighting in Houdini. First, you will identify and use the core light types: point, spot, area, and environment. That means recognizing when a scene needs an omnidirectional source, a focused cone of light, a surface emitter for soft shadows, or an HDRI for realistic reflections. Second, you will set up an environment light with an HDRI for realistic global illumination. This skill helps you produce accurate reflections on metals and coherent ambient light across the scene. Third, you will control key parameters such as color, intensity, exposure, and decay so that brightness, hue, and falloff behave predictably. Practically, you will learn how exposure interacts with intensity and how quadratic decay produces natural falloff. Fourth, you will implement basic light linking to specify which lights affect which objects, useful for isolating a character from a busy background. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify the skill with a render or a light-link configuration. As you progress, ask yourself: which light best reveals material properties, and how does decay change perceived distance? These questions will guide your experimentation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
screens.subtitle: How to verify and practice each objective

narration.text: This second objectives page gives you practical checks to verify competency. For identifying and using light types, practice by swapping a point and area light and observing shadow hardness and reflected highlights; a point light makes hard shadows while an area light softens edges. For HDRI environment setup, load a neutral studio HDRI and adjust rotation and intensity; verify reflections on a metallic sphere and lower the HDRI intensity until the scene reads balanced. For tuning color, intensity, exposure and decay, perform three short renders: one with exaggerated intensity, one with exposure adjustment, and one with quadratic decay enabled. Compare results to learn how exposure relates to perceived brightness and how decay restores natural falloff. For light linking, use the Light Linker to turn a key light off for a background object; if the object loses the key's sharp highlight while the subject keeps it, your links are correct. Each check is a small render or toggle you can use as a milestone. These hands-on checks will make the abstract parameters concrete and build confidence for more complex scenes.

screens.title: Why lighting defines realism
screens.subtitle: Light reveals form, materials, and depth

narration.text: Lighting is more than illumination: it's the primary way our eyes read shape, texture, and spatial relationships. When a light hits a surface it creates highlights, midtones, and shadows. Those three tonal regions tell the viewer about curvature, material roughness, and surface imperfections. For example, a small bright point light on a metallic sphere creates a sharp specular highlight and crisp shadow edges, which signals a hard, glossy material. By contrast, a large area light will produce broad highlights and soft shadows, implying diffuse or softer surfaces. A common misconception is that more lights equal better lighting. In practice, indiscriminate lights flatten a scene and increase render cost; purposeful placement — key, fill, and rim — provides separation and depth with fewer sources. Understand that HDRI environment light supplies global, scene-wide illumination and color bounce that smaller lights cannot replicate. For practical work, always start by defining the goal: silhouette, texture, or reflection fidelity. Then choose a light type and tune size, exposure and decay to serve that goal. As a quick check, if your subject loses shape, reduce fill or lower HDRI intensity to restore contrast and reveal form. What single change could most improve your current render?

keyIdea.title: Lighting defines visual information
keyIdea.text: Use light to reveal form, not just brighten the scene. Strategic light placement sculpts material and depth while keeping renders efficient.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why lighting defines realism
Light sculpts highlights, midtones, and shadows that communicate material and shape.
  • Highlights show surface gloss and curvature.
  • Shadows provide depth and anchor objects to the scene.
  • HDRI offers global cues that small lights cannot reproduce.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize light roles: key for form, fill for shadow control, rim for separation, environment for context.

Illustrative examples
Small Point
Sharp specular highlight, crisp shadow edges — suggests hard, glossy surface.
Large Area
Broad highlight, soft shadow falloff — suggests softer material and gentle illumination.
Environment (HDRI)
Provides reflections and consistent ambient color that tie objects into the scene.
Common mistake
Using many high-intensity lights without role leads to flat images and wasted render time.
Pro tip: Assign each light a clear purpose and test by disabling all but one to understand its contribution.

screens.title: Creating and placing lights in Houdini
screens.subtitle: Add lights in the obj context and use param panels to tune them

narration.text: Adding lights in Houdini is a straightforward process, and learning the workflow helps you iterate quickly. In the object context, you can access 'Lights and Cameras' from the top menu or press Tab in the network editor and type 'light' to create a new light node. Once created, select the node to open its parameter panel. Key parameters you will adjust are color, intensity, exposure, decay and any type-specific controls like cone angle for spot lights or size for area lights. A good practice is to place a light, make one parameter change, then render to observe the effect. This isolates cause and effect. Example workflow: create an area light for your key; position it above and to the side of your subject; set size to introduce soft shadows; increase intensity or exposure until the subject reads correctly in the histogram; then add a lower-intensity area as a fill. Misconception to avoid: moving lights without checking exposure can hide whether the light is too dim or too bright. Always iterate with small renders and use isolation renders — render only one light at a time — to confirm contributions. How will you structure a quick test to evaluate a newly created light?

keyIdea.title: Iterative placement
keyIdea.text: Create, adjust one parameter, and render. Isolate lights to understand their individual contributions before combining them.

content.html:
Process Flow
Creating and placing lights
A step-by-step routine to add lights and tune parameters.
  1. Create a light in obj context using the menu or Tab menu.
  2. Open the parameter panel and choose type: Point, Spot, Area, or Environment.
  3. Position and orient the light; set size for area lights and cone angle for spots.
  4. Tune intensity/exposure and enable quadratic decay for realistic falloff.
  5. Render single-light isolations, then combine lights and refine balance.
Example: create an area light above a sphere, size it to soften shadows, set intensity to 1200, then add a low-intensity fill at 25% of key.
Check: can you produce a visible silhouette without overexposing highlights?
Practice Panel
Use this checklist every time you add a new light:
  • Does it serve a role (key, fill, rim, environment)?
  • Is decay set appropriately for scene scale?
  • Do shadows have the correct hardness for the intended material?
Pro Tip
Use isolation renders and the Render View's exposure controls to judge brightness rather than relying on viewport lighting alone.

screens.title: Point vs Spot vs Area lights
screens.subtitle: Choose the right emitter for highlights, focus, and soft shadows

narration.text: Understanding the behavioral differences between point, spot and area lights helps you pick the right tool quickly. A point light emits equally in all directions from a single point. Use it for a localized source such as a lamp bulb or a small highlight. A common mistake is using a point light when you want soft shadows; because it has no physical size its shadows are hard-edged. A spot light emits inside a cone and gives you directional control; it is excellent for rim or stage lighting where you need to constrain illumination. Spots include cone angle and penumbra controls to feather edges. An area light emits from a surface and produces natural soft shadows and smoother highlights because of its size; it is ideal for simulating windows, softboxes, or broad sky patches. Example: to light a portrait model, use an area light as the key for soft facial shadows, a low-intensity area as fill on the opposite side, and a small spot behind the subject as a rim to separate them from the background. When in doubt about shadow softness, increase emitter size rather than intensity. Which emitter will best communicate your subject's material qualities?

keyIdea.title: Pick by physical behavior
keyIdea.text: Point for compact bright sources, spot for directional cones, area for soft, realistic shadows and broad illumination.

content.html:
Point Light
Omnidirectional
Emits equally in all directions from a single point. Good for small, bright sources and sharp highlights.
Common use: lamp bulb, spark.
Spot Light
Conical & directional
Shaped cone with cone angle and penumbra. Use for focused beams and rim highlights.
Common use: flashlight, stage spot.
Area Light
Surface emitter
Emits from a defined surface. Larger size softens shadows and creates realistic highlights for materials.
Common use: window light, softbox.
Example Scenario
Portrait model: Area light as key for soft facial shadows, area fill at low intensity, spot as thin rim behind subject for separation. If reflections are needed, add an HDRI environment.
Common Mistake
Relying on intensity to soften shadows instead of increasing emitter size creates unrealistic highlights.

screens.title: Environment Light and HDRI
screens.subtitle: Image-based lighting for reflections and global illumination

narration.text: An Environment Light in Houdini uses a high dynamic range image to wrap the scene in real-world lighting information. HDRIs contain a wide range of brightness values captured from a real location, from very bright sun spots to dim sky regions. When used as an environment map, this data provides both illumination and accurate reflections, especially important for metallic or glossy materials. To use an HDRI, load it into the Environment Map parameter and rotate the map to change where the brightest regions fall relative to your subject. A practical example: place an HDRI with a studio softbox and subtle window light, then lower the environment intensity to serve as a gentle fill while an area key sculpts facial detail. A common misconception is that HDRIs replace the need for local lights — they do not. HDRIs provide ambient context and reflections but local area or spot lights remain essential to shape and emphasize features. When baking for game engines, HDRIs are often used to build light probes; in Houdini they are excellent for previewing realistic behavior during look development. What does your HDRI reveal about material detail in your scene?

keyIdea.title: HDRI = context + reflection
keyIdea.text: Use an environment map to add realistic ambient illumination and reflections; combine with local lights for artistic control.

content.html:
Definition
Environment Light & HDRI
Load an HDRI into the Environment Map parameter to provide rich global lighting and reflections.
Key controls: Map file, Rotation, Intensity/Exposure. Rotate the map to reposition bright areas and adjust intensity to balance with local lights.
Example
Use a neutral studio HDRI at low intensity for ambient fill, then add an area key for form. Verify reflections on metallic objects for realism.
Architecture of usage
HDRI Map
360° image with high dynamic range values for accurate lighting.
Environment Light Node
Wraps the HDRI around the scene and feeds lighting/reflection data to the renderer.
Rotation
Orients the HDRI to place dominant highlights where needed.
Intensity / Exposure
Controls HDRI brightness relative to local lights.
Tip: combine HDRI for ambient information with local lights for controlled sculpting of form and reflections.

screens.title: Key light parameters: color, intensity, exposure, decay
screens.subtitle: How parameters interact and example settings

narration.text: Lights are controlled by a small set of parameters that interact in predictable ways. Color sets the hue of emitted light and directly affects diffuse shading and reflections. Intensity and exposure both change brightness but behave differently: intensity is a linear multiplier of emitted energy while exposure acts like a photographic f-stop, shifting the overall brightness in a camera-relative manner. Decay models falloff with distance; quadratic decay — the default physical model — reduces intensity proportional to the square of distance. Practically, start by choosing an approximate intensity, then refine exposure to match camera response. For example, an area key might use intensity in the thousands for scene scale, with exposure between 0 and 2 to fine-tune without changing color dynamics. If objects appear equally lit regardless of distance, check that decay is not disabled. Misconception: exposure is not a replacement for decay — exposure brightens uniformly, decay creates distance-based realism. Below is a simple parameter snapshot you might use during look development. Use isolation renders to confirm each parameter's visible effect. Key light parameters: color, intensity, exposure, decay means tune intensity and exposure to control brightness, and enable quadratic decay for realistic distance falloff.. In practical terms, how parameters interact and example settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parameters work together
keyIdea.text: Tune intensity and exposure to control brightness, and enable quadratic decay for realistic distance falloff.

content.html:
Definition
Key parameters
Understand how color, intensity, exposure and decay change rendered results and how to balance them.
Light {
  type: "area"
  color: "#ffffff"
  intensity: 1500
  exposure: 1
  decay: "quadratic"
  size: [1.2, 0.8]
}
Explanation & example
  • Color affects both diffuse tint and reflections; use warm or cool hues intentionally.
  • Intensity sets raw emitted energy; exposure shifts perceived brightness for camera matching.
  • Quadratic decay models real-world falloff; disable only for stylized effects.
Key Takeaway
Adjust intensity then exposure, and keep quadratic decay enabled for realistic distance falloff unless you need a stylized look.
Misconception check: If shadows remain equally bright as you move objects away from the light, decay is likely disabled.

screens.title: Decay and Quadratic Decay explained
screens.subtitle: Why distance-based falloff matters for realism

narration.text: Decay defines how quickly light intensity decreases as distance increases. The physically correct model is quadratic decay, where intensity falls off in proportion to the square of the distance. Practically, that means doubling the distance from a light reduces its intensity to one quarter. Quadratic decay creates believable shadow transitions and prevents distant objects from appearing unnaturally bright. If you disable decay, lights will illuminate everything equally, producing flat and unrealistic images. That can be useful intentionally for certain stylized or technical passes, but it is not a substitute for proper placement and exposure. Example: in a room scene, enabling quadratic decay will make near objects much brighter than far ones, matching real-world perception. When tuning decay, also adjust light size and exposure because soft shadows and perceived brightness depend on their combined effect. A common pitfall is raising intensity to compensate for decay without checking exposure; that can push highlights out of range. Always test with a neutral gray sphere to judge falloff and reflectivity — it’s a reliable probe for decay behavior. How will you test decay in your next scene?

keyIdea.title: Use decay for natural falloff
keyIdea.text: Quadratic decay gives realistic distance-based dimming. Disable only for deliberate stylistic or technical reasons.

content.html:
Core Concept
Decay & Quadratic Decay
Quadratic decay reduces intensity proportional to distance squared, producing natural-looking falloff.
Practical check: place a neutral gray sphere at multiple distances from a light and compare brightness. With quadratic decay, brightness will fall quickly with distance; without it, brightness will stay uniform.
Example & pitfalls
Example: set an area key at moderate intensity with quadratic decay enabled. Objects near the key will have strong modeling light while distant props remain subtly lit by the environment.
Pitfall
Turning decay off and then raising intensity creates flat illumination and hides depth cues.
Try: toggle decay on and off during single-light renders to directly observe its impact.

screens.title: Light linking with the Light Linker
screens.subtitle: Control which lights affect which objects for artistic isolation

narration.text: Light linking gives you fine-grained control over illumination by specifying which lights include or exclude specific objects. By default, every light affects every object, but complex scenes benefit from selective linking: a character may need a dramatic key while the background remains subtly lit. In Houdini, open the Light Linker panel (Windows > Light Linker) to create these relationships. The workflow is simple: select a light, choose target objects, then include or exclude the light per object. A common use is excluding a strong key from the background to prevent overexposure. Another is pairing a rim spot to affect only the subject to create separation without affecting reflections on nearby props. Misconception: light linking is only for optimization — it is primarily an artistic tool to craft readable images. Example: create an area key for subject, then exclude it from background objects; add a low-intensity environment light to keep background visible without the key's strong influence. Light linking also reduces wasted shading calculations if used thoughtfully, improving render times in large scenes. What selective link would most improve your current composition?

keyIdea.title: Artistic isolation with links
keyIdea.text: Use the Light Linker to include or exclude lights per object so each element receives only the intended illumination.

content.html:
Process Flow
Light Linking workflow
  1. Open Windows > Light Linker.
  2. Select a light node you want to control.
  3. Choose target objects and mark include or exclude settings.
  4. Render to verify the light affects only the intended objects.
Example: exclude the key light from the floor grid so the subject keeps dramatic modeling while the floor remains softly lit by environment light.
Cards — Why link?
Artistic control: isolate highlights to subject without affecting background.
Optimization: avoid costly light calculations on objects that do not need the light.
Debugging: toggle links to see single-light contributions easily.
Try: disable a light for a single object and note the difference in a small render to learn each light's contribution.

screens.title: Three-point lighting with HDRI
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step build: environment fill, key area, fill area, rim spot

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through a classic three-point lighting setup combined with an HDRI environment for realistic fill. Start a new scene and place a grid as a floor and a sphere as the subject. Assign a principled shader with moderate roughness for visible reflections. Step one: create an Environment Light and load an HDRI, lower the intensity to around 0.3–0.6 to provide subtle ambient fill and reflections. Step two: add an Area Light as the key, position it above and to one side, set size for soft shadows, and set intensity to a working value such as 1000–3000 depending on scale; then adjust exposure by small increments. Step three: add a second Area Light opposite the key at 20–30% intensity to fill shadows gently. Step four: add a Spot Light behind the subject as a rim, tune cone and penumbra for a thin highlight to separate the silhouette. Finally, use the Light Linker to exclude the rim from background geometry if necessary. Misconception: HDRI is not a replacement for the key — it provides context while area and spot lights sculpt the subject. Render iterations between each step help you see incremental contributions and speed learning. What single tweak would you try first to improve contrast?

keyIdea.title: Combine HDRI with three-point
keyIdea.text: Use HDRI for ambient context and three-point local lights for sculpting form. Iterate renders step-by-step.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Three-point lighting with HDRI
Follow these steps in your scene and render after each to learn contributions.
Step 1 — Environment (Fill)
Load HDRI, set intensity low (0.3–0.6), rotate to position main highlights for reflections.
Step 2 — Key (Area)
Place above and to the side, size to soften shadows, set intensity according to scene scale.
Step 3 — Fill (Area)
Opposite side at 20–30% of key to soften shadows without flattening shape.
Step 4 — Rim (Spot)
Place behind subject, tune cone angle and penumbra to create a thin edge highlight.
Key Takeaway
Render iteratively after each step to learn how each light shapes form. Use Light Linker to isolate rim or key from background when needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Lighting Fundamentals

narration.text: Let's summarize the central ideas to carry forward. First, identify the right light type: point for compact highlights, spot for directional cones, area for soft, realistic shadows, and environment lights for image-based global illumination. Second, HDRIs power reflections and ambient color, but they don't replace local lights used to shape form and emphasize features. Third, key parameters — color, intensity, exposure, and decay — interact; start with intensity, then refine exposure, and keep quadratic decay on for physical falloff unless you have a specific artistic reason to disable it. Fourth, light linking is a practical artistic control that lets you include or exclude lights per object to avoid unwanted highlights and to optimize render work. Keep these points in mind when building scenes: define roles for lights, iterate with isolated renders, and use small tests like a neutral sphere to judge material and decay. Which of these concepts will you apply first in your next lighting pass?

keyIdea.title: Essential reminders
keyIdea.text: Choose correct light types, use HDRI for context, tune parameters thoughtfully, and use light linking for precision.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three compact reminders from this chapter.
Light Types
Point, Spot, Area, Environment: pick by physical behavior and intended effect.
HDRI
Environment maps provide reflections and global illumination; combine with local lights to sculpt form.
Parameters & Decay
Tune color, intensity, exposure and keep quadratic decay for realistic falloff; test with small renders.
Summary Takeaway
Think in roles: environment for context, area/spot for sculpting, use light linking to isolate and optimize.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders to use during look development

narration.text: Before you finish, lock these three reminders into your practice. One: always assign each light a role — key, fill, rim, or environment — and avoid adding lights without intention. Two: use HDRIs to provide realistic reflections and ambient color, but combine them with local lights for shape and emphasis. Three: render iteratively, isolating single lights and testing decay and exposure; small probes like a neutral sphere reveal how parameters behave. Use light linking to maintain control in complex scenes and to avoid accidental overexposure of background elements. These compact rules will save time and improve visual consistency as you refine materials and lighting. Which reminder will be your first check during the next render pass? What to Remember means assign light roles, combine hdri with local lights, iterate with isolation renders and use light linking for control.. In practical terms, three quick reminders to use during look development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical reminders
keyIdea.text: Assign light roles, combine HDRI with local lights, iterate with isolation renders and use light linking for control.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What to Remember
What to Remember
Three quick rules to guide every lighting pass.
Role First
Give each light a purpose and disable extras that don't serve the image.
HDRI + Local
Use HDRI for context and reflections, and local lights to model form and emphasis.
Iterate & Isolate
Render one light at a time to learn its effect and ensure decay and exposure behave as expected.
Keep these rules visible in every lighting session to maintain consistent, efficient look development.
